assessment.nobel_worthiness: A clean case of theory anticipating a new quantum state of matter: the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model predicted flat bands at a magic twist angle, and experiment then found correlated insulators and superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene. It opened moire quantum materials as a tunable platform. As someone who watched graphene overturn expectations, this is the kind of surprise I want to recognise, and theory and measurement are tightly linked.
assessment.attribution: The theory pair (Bistritzer, MacDonald) and the experimental leader (Jarillo-Herrero) form a natural three-way split between prediction and discovery. The experimental first author and other groups' contributions (e.g. early twist-angle work and related theory) may be argued, but the supplied names support a fair configuration.
assessment.maturity: Experimental results have been reproduced by many independent groups since 2018 across transport, scanning probes and spectroscopy, and the single-particle theory is well established. The nature of the correlated and superconducting states is still debated, but the core discovery is stable. Timing is arguably early but defensible.
uncertainties: The pairing mechanism of the superconductivity and the origin of the correlated states are unresolved.
Credit to the lead experimental student and to other twist-angle theory contributors is not captured in the credited names; my recollection of the history is not independently verified.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance and then giant MgO-based tunnel junctions are a pillar of spintronics and underlie read heads and MRAM. The physics (spin-dependent tunnelling and coherent symmetry filtering) is well understood and quantitative, which suits my own field of magnetism and electronic-structure theory. A Nobel link to magnetism with real technological reach.
assessment.attribution: Moodera and Miyazaki independently reported large room-temperature TMR in 1995. Parkin and Yuasa/Djayaprawira (with Butler and Mathon providing the first-principles prediction of coherent tunnelling) made the MgO breakthrough in 2004. The supplied trio covers the amorphous-barrier discovery and Parkin's MgO work, but the MgO experimentalists and the theorists Butler and Mathon are absent, so the allocation is not fully clean.
assessment.maturity: Highly mature and heavily commercialised, confirmed independently for over twenty years; some argue recognition was partly covered by the 2007 GMR prize, which is a timing and overlap concern rather than a scientific one.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2007 prize for giant magnetoresistance could weigh against it.
Omission of Yuasa, Djayaprawira, Butler and Mathon complicates a fair three-person split.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamical mean-field theory is the workhorse for treating strongly correlated electrons beyond band theory, and with DFT+DMFT it connects first-principles electronic structure to Mott physics and spectra in real materials. Its conceptual originality, in the infinite-dimension limit and the local self-energy picture, and its broad use make it a major theoretical contribution that I know well from my own field.
assessment.attribution: Metzner and Vollhardt founded the infinite-dimension limit, and Georges and Kotliar constructed the DMFT mapping to an impurity problem; Muller-Hartmann also contributed. The supplied trio is credible, but Walter Metzner, a key originator, is not in the credited names, which leaves the allocation contestable.
assessment.maturity: Decades of use and cross-validation against experiment and numerically exact methods; limits (non-local correlations, quantitative accuracy in some materials) are known. A mature, stable framework.
uncertainties: The omission of Metzner and Muller-Hartmann weakens a clean attribution.
Nobel committees have historically been cautious about method-oriented theory with indirect experimental decisiveness.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators created a new classification of electronic matter and a thriving experimental field; the prediction, the HgTe confirmation and the later 3D materials are a model of theory meeting experiment. The 2016 prize recognised topological phases but not this discovery specifically.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the original prediction; Molenkamp led the HgTe quantum-well observation, following the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal. Bernevig and Zhang (deceased) and the 3D TI experimentalists (Hasan, Cava) complicate the picture, so the supplied three are a defensible but incomplete configuration.
assessment.maturity: Independently confirmed many times with material-specific realisations, and the interpretation is stable. The topic is mature but may be perceived as partly covered by the 2016 prize.
uncertainties: Possible perceived overlap with the 2016 topological phases prize.
Credit split between the 2D (Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang) and 3D discoveries is not resolved by the supplied names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, with magic-wavelength trapping proposed by Katori, deliver the best fractional stability and accuracy of any measurement, with consequences for redefining the second, relativistic geodesy and tests of fundamental physics. The physics is clear and quantitative, and the results have been verified in many laboratories.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and Ye drove the performance frontier with strontium clocks; a two-person award is natural. Hall and Hansch recognised frequency combs in 2005 and ion-clock work was recognised in 2012, so the lattice clock contribution is distinct.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed by multiple national laboratories and clock comparisons; redefinition of the second is expected, which makes the timing reasonable.
uncertainties: Other contributors (e.g. Ludlow, Lemonde, Bloom and early strontium work) could be argued for.
Close relation to the thorium nuclear clock candidate may split recognition.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The discovery that magnetic order survives down to monolayers in van der Waals crystals (CrI3 and Cr2Ge2Te6) addresses the old Mermin-Wagner question in a concrete, materials-based way and opens new routes to spintronic devices. It is closely tied to my own interests in 2D and van der Waals magnets, and I am drawn to it.
assessment.attribution: The two nearly simultaneous 2017 Nature papers came from the Xu group (CrI3 with Jarillo-Herrero) and the Zhang group (Cr2Ge2Te6). Jarillo-Herrero is also credited here but I would keep him with the twisted bilayer candidate, so a two-person configuration is chosen. Credit is shared with other contributors, which makes the allocation delicate.
assessment.maturity: Rapidly expanding field with many independent confirmations, but it is young; device applicability and microscopic theory of the magnetism are still developing, so this is likely premature.
uncertainties: Likely premature relative to other condensed matter candidates.
Allocation among three groups and the theory of anisotropy-stabilised 2D order are unsettled.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realise Hubbard-type models with exact control, observing the superfluid-Mott transition and enabling quantum simulation of many-body physics that is hard for classical theory. It is a clear case where theory (Jaksch and Zoller) and experiment together expanded what we can test about correlated matter.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch) proposed the Bose-Hubbard realisation; Greiner and Bloch observed the Mott transition (with Hansch); Esslinger advanced fermionic lattices. Jaksch is not credited, and Hansch and Esslinger complicate the selection, so the trio is one of several plausible configurations.
assessment.maturity: Mature and widely reproduced, though the simulation payoff beyond what classical methods can do is still being established.
uncertainties: Competition for recognition among several AMO candidates and unresolved allocation (Esslinger, Jaksch).
Whether quantum advantage over classical simulation has been shown is not settled.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Aberration-corrected electron microscopy gave sub-angstrom imaging of atoms in real materials and is now routine for materials physics and spectroscopy; it ties directly to the experimental data against which electronic-structure theory is tested. Its practical impact is large and the underlying optics is original and clear.
assessment.attribution: Rose provided the theory of correction, Haider and Urban built the correctors and demonstrated their use; Krivanek is a major absentee from the credited names, which makes a fair allocation harder. The three supplied names are a plausible configuration given the Kavli Prize history, which I recall but have not verified here.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature, widely deployed and independently confirmed; timing is late rather than premature.
uncertainties: The omission of Ondrej Krivanek is a significant attribution gap.
Might be seen as an instrumentation or chemistry-adjacent prize rather than a physical discovery.
